classification_notes: Montalbano describes 718 as pulling from English, Italian, Dutch, humanist and geometric sources at once, which puts it closer to a broad humanist grotesque than any single historical sans model.
summary: A twelve-weight humanist grotesque named after Brooklyn's phone code, built to hold its own in both text and display.
description: 718 mixes English, Italian and Dutch sans-serif habits with humanist and geometric touches, giving it a personality a straight grotesque would not have. Twelve weights from Extra Thin to Ultra each come with a matching italic and a full set of OpenType figures, fractions and small caps. Montalbano built it as a text face first, with enough character to carry display sizes too.
foundry_blurb: Terminal Design frame 718 as a nod to Brooklyn's area code and, in James Montalbano's words, the real New York as opposed to Manhattan. The foundry credits it with a mix of English, Italian, Dutch, humanist and geometric influences, working well as a text face with real personality in display.

name: Alfon
classification_notes: Cupped serifs and chamfered corners put Alfon in serif territory despite its blunt, sturdy forms. Montalbano pitches it as the serif counterpart to his sans-serif Giacomo, so the given brief's Sans label has been corrected here.
summary: A muscular serif with chamfered corners and cupped serifs, built to read well as text and show personality at large sizes.
description: Alfon takes the sturdy, blunt character of Montalbano's sans-serif Giacomo and rebuilds it in serif form, with chamfered corners and cupped serif ends adding bite at display sizes. Four weights from Regular to Heavy each carry a loose, slightly funky italic. It works as a readable text face while keeping enough edge for headlines.
foundry_blurb: Montalbano calls Alfon a modern, muscular typeface, filled with subtle details that let it work as a readable text face while offering plenty of personality at large sizes. He pairs it with Giacomo as a serif companion, with chamfered corners and cupped serifs, plus a flowing, slightly funky italic.

name: Badinage
classification_notes: A connecting script with unusual joins between letters. It ships with a separate set of plain capitals so all-caps setting avoids the flourishes that usually trip up script faces.
summary: A vertical connecting script with eight weights and a set of plain capitals built specifically for all-caps setting.
description: Badinage grew out of logo sketches, with letterform connections odd enough that Montalbano felt compelled to finish the design. It ships in eight weights from Thin to Black, and includes a set of plain capitals so all-caps text avoids the flourishes and connecting strokes that usually get in the way when scripts are set in caps. Multiple OpenType stylistic sets and contextual alternates handle the beginnings and ends of words.
foundry_blurb: Terminal Design describe Badinage as a vertical connecting script born from logo exploration sketches. Montalbano was drawn to the odd way the letterforms connected, and built in a set of plain capitals for all-caps setting, since flourishes that suit lowercase tend to work against a design set in caps.

name: Berrymond Display
classification_notes: Developed from a 1968 book-title commission and later expanded into a full display face. The foundry is explicit that it is not intended for text setting; only a single weight is offered.
summary: A large-format display face grown from a 1968 book-title commission for John Berryman's Dream Songs, with an unusually wide Greek and Cyrillic range for a display face.
description: Farrar Straus Giroux commissioned Terminal Design to letter John Berryman's book titles, based on the 1968 Dream Songs jacket design. Montalbano later expanded that alphabet into a full display typeface, admitting he got carried away with it. It covers extended Latin plus monotonic and polytonic Greek and Cyrillic, but is built for large sizes only.
foundry_blurb: Terminal Design trace Berrymond Display back to a commission from Farrar Straus Giroux for new lettering on John Berryman's book titles, based on the 1968 Dream Songs jacket. Montalbano expanded the alphabet into a full typeface, by his own account getting carried away with it, and is clear it is a display face rather than a text one.

name: Bryce Canyon Sans
classification_notes: Based on hand-cut lettering found throughout Bryce Canyon National Park. The source material was uppercase-only, so Montalbano drew a full lowercase and extended the language support himself.
summary: A rustic sans built from hand-cut lettering found across Bryce Canyon National Park, expanded from an uppercase-only source into a full two-weight family.
description: Montalbano based Bryce Canyon Sans on hand-cut signage lettering he found throughout the park. The original reference was capitals only, so he drew a lowercase to match and broadened the character set to cover Vietnamese and most European languages. A bold weight was added late in development, alongside the original regular.
foundry_blurb: Terminal Design describe Bryce Canyon Sans as based on hand-cut lettering found throughout Bryce Canyon National Park. The original was uppercase-only with limited language coverage; Montalbano added a lowercase and extended coverage to Vietnamese and most European languages, with a bold weight added toward the end of the project.

name: Cappella
classification_notes: Grew out of a one-weight, all-caps custom job for Fordham Chapel based on wood-carved letters. The lowercase folds in calligraphic details from Montalbano's earlier work rather than following the caps mechanically.
summary: A ten-weight serif built from the idiosyncratic character of wood-carved chapel lettering, with a lowercase drawn to match rather than a straight mechanical expansion.
description: Cappella began as a single-weight, all-caps custom design for Fordham Chapel, based on wood-carved letters Montalbano found idiosyncratic enough to want to develop further. The lowercase blends details lifted from the uppercase with calligraphic moves from his earlier work. Montalbano is upfront that it will not suit every job, but calls the result fresh and interesting.
foundry_blurb: Terminal Design trace Cappella to a custom Fordham Chapel commission, a one-weight all-caps design based on wood-carved letters. Montalbano became interested in the idiosyncrasy of the carved forms and built out a lowercase blending uppercase details with calligraphic moves from earlier work, describing the result as not right for every job but fresh and interesting.

name: Choice Sans
classification_notes: Built around slightly squared counter shapes borrowed from Montalbano's Clearview work, aiming at high legibility on screen and in print. Sold in three widths, standard, condensed and compressed, with an oblique for every weight.
summary: A true square sans serif in three widths and twelve weights each, drawn from the counter shapes Montalbano developed for Clearview.
description: Choice Sans takes the slightly squared counters Montalbano developed for his Clearview signage system and builds them into a general-purpose sans. Twelve weights from Extra Thin to Ultra come in three widths, standard, condensed and compressed, each with a matching oblique, for 72 fonts across the family. Montalbano uses it as his own email-client font and pitches it for jobs where legibility matters most.
foundry_blurb: Terminal Design present Choice Sans as a true square sans serif design, its counter shapes drawn from the Clearview system. Montalbano notes the family runs to 72 fonts across three widths and twelve weights with obliques, and says it has the potential to perform well wherever legibility is the main concern; he uses it in his own email client.

name: ClearviewADA
classification_notes: A genuine signage and wayfinding typeface, derived from ClearviewText and adjusted to meet US Americans with Disabilities Act stroke-width-to-height and glyph proportion requirements. Also sold in a condensed width. Categorised here as sans-serif per house convention, since Signage is not one of our category options.
summary: A signage and wayfinding sans built off ClearviewText, adjusted to meet the stroke and glyph proportions required under US ADA guidelines.
description: ClearviewADA takes the ClearviewText design and reworks its proportions to satisfy Americans with Disabilities Act requirements for stroke width to height and glyph height to width. It comes in five weights with italics and a condensed width, and reads well in both text and display use on signage. It sits within Terminal Design's wider Clearview system, in development since 1995.
foundry_blurb: Terminal Design position ClearviewADA as derived from ClearviewText and specifically designed for signage and wayfinding, built to meet US Americans with Disabilities Act guidelines for stroke width to height and glyph height to width ratios, while still working across text and display uses.

name: ClearviewHwy
classification_notes: The famous US highway signage typeface. Developed from 1995 with extensive human-factors testing and granted interim approval by the Federal Highway Administration in 2004. Weight and contrast are designated by a numbered series (1 to 6, positive and negative-contrast W/B cuts) rather than named weights, built for retroreflective road signs rather than general text. Categorised here as sans-serif per house convention, since Roadway is not one of our category options.
summary: The Clearview highway signage typeface, developed from 1995 through human-factors research and granted interim approval by the US Federal Highway Administration in 2004.
description: ClearviewHwy is the road-sign face at the centre of the Clearview system, built from research into legibility for aging drivers. Testing showed it delivered 12 to 29 percent better legibility than the road-sign fonts it was designed to replace. It ships in numbered positive and negative-contrast cuts, from 1 to 6, rather than named weights, matched to specific sign types and viewing distances.
foundry_blurb: Terminal Design describe ClearviewHwy as the product of work on the Clearview system for text, display, roadway and interior guide signage that Montalbano began in 1995, based on human factors research aimed at reducing visibility problems for aging drivers. Testing showed between 12 and 29 percent more legibility than the fonts it was designed to replace, and the US Federal Highway Administration granted interim approval for federal roadway use in 2004.

name: ClearviewText
classification_notes: Built from the research behind ClearviewHwy but tuned for text and general use rather than roadway signs. Sold in standard, compressed and condensed widths, and replaces Terminal Design's earlier ClearviewOne family.
summary: A text-oriented sans built from the legibility research behind the Clearview highway system, with enough character to stand apart from the wider field of grotesques.
description: ClearviewText carries the legibility research behind ClearviewHwy into general text and display use, and Montalbano says it reads astonishingly well as a text face. Eight weights from ExtraThin to Black each carry an italic, and the family is available in standard, compressed and condensed widths. It replaces Terminal Design's earlier ClearviewOne family, and includes small caps, oldstyle and lining figures, and arbitrary fractions.
foundry_blurb: Terminal Design present ClearviewText as the continuing evolution of the Clearview family, drawing on the research behind the ultra-legible ClearviewHwy fonts while carrying enough of its own character to stand apart from the wider field of sans serifs. The 48-font family replaces the earlier ClearviewOne collection, and Montalbano's Clearview work sits in the permanent collection of the Smithsonian Cooper-Hewitt National Design Museum.

name: Consul
classification_notes: Montalbano calls it a French Modern serif, though colleague Charles Nix reads it closer to a Scotch Roman. Loosely based on 19th-century Didot specimens by Gustav Mayeur rather than a direct revival. Sold across four optical sizes, Caption, Text, Deck and Display, tuned for their respective size ranges. Recategorised here as serif; the original brief's Text/Display label was not a valid category on its own.
summary: A four-optical-size serif that grew from a display design for Men's Vogue, pitched by its designer as a French Modern with a strong Didot streak.
description: Consul started life as a display design Montalbano drew for Men's Vogue, loosely inspired by 19th-century Didot specimens from the Parisian printer Gustav Mayeur, though it stops short of being a revival. Montalbano spent most of 2008 optically sizing it across four ranges, Caption, Text, Deck and Display, with soft, curved serif points and severely angled italics. Alternate a, e, g, r and s forms give it several different personalities within one family.
foundry_blurb: Terminal Design trace Consul back to a display design Montalbano created for Men's Vogue, describing it as a French Modern serif, though colleague Charles Nix reads it closer to a Scotch Roman. It draws on 19th-century Didot specimens by Parisian printer Gustav Mayeur without being a revival, and Montalbano spent most of 2008 developing it as an optically sized family across Caption, Text, Deck and Display ranges.

name: Enclave
classification_notes: Explicitly pitched by the designer as a slab serif that avoids the heavy 19th-century Egyptian slab tradition. Proportions run narrow in the lighter weights, though no separate condensed product is sold. Recategorised here as slab rather than the original brief's Serif label, since the designer specifically calls it out as a slab-serif design.
summary: A slab serif built to shed the heavy 19th-century Egyptian character that limits most slabs, with narrow proportions in its lighter weights and lively italics throughout.
description: Enclave grew from work on how to set large passages of slab-serif text without the bulk of the 19th-century Egyptian tradition. Eight weights from Thin to Black run noticeably narrow at the lighter end, each with a matching italic, and Montalbano built in graduated weight steps meant for editorial and corporate work.
foundry_blurb: Terminal Design call Enclave a distinctive slab serif that shakes off the 19th-century Egyptian characteristics that have limited the range and appeal of slab serifs in general, with condensed proportions in the lighter weights, graduated weight steps and lively italics suited to editorial and corporate use.

name: Fervent
classification_notes: Pitched by the designer as the sans-serif companion to his script Badinage, translating some of that script's lowercase details. Its roman forms borrow from italic shapes, giving it unusual motion for a sans. Recategorised here as sans-serif; the design itself is not a script despite its script parentage.
summary: The sans-serif companion to Badinage, with roman forms that borrow from italic shapes and a run of alternate letters that push it past any one sans category.
description: Fervent takes the unadorned alternate capitals from Montalbano's script typeface Badinage and rebuilds the concept as a sans, carrying over details like the epsilon-shaped e and the forms of a, n, m and k. The roman weights lean on italic structure for a sense of motion rare in a sans, and alternates for a, e, g, r and s open up several personalities within the ten-weight family.
foundry_blurb: Terminal Design position Fervent as the sans serif version of Badinage, translating alternate uppercase forms and lowercase details from the script into a sans built with romans that borrow heavily from italic shapes. Montalbano suggests the result may be beyond any sans serif category, working equally well in text as in display.

name: Giacomo 2.0
classification_notes: Montalbano is explicit that Giacomo 2.0 is a sans serif that resists standard classification, sitting outside geometric, humanist and grotesque models. Chamfered corners and cupped terminals add softness at larger sizes. Notable as Terminal Design's first OpenType design with Cyrillic support. Recategorised here as sans-serif; the original brief's Script label does not match the designer's own description.
summary: A sans serif that Montalbano deliberately built to dodge the usual geometric, humanist and grotesque boxes, with chamfered corners and cupped terminals that soften at larger sizes.
description: Giacomo 2.0 sits in what its designer calls a familiar yet unique space, neither geometric nor humanist nor grotesque. Chamfered corners and cupped terminals are barely visible at small sizes but add real softness in display use, across six weights from Light to Black with italics. It was Terminal Design's first OpenType release to include Cyrillic.
foundry_blurb: Terminal Design describe Giacomo 2.0 as a sans serif design that cannot be easily categorised, not geometric, not really humanist and certainly not a grotesque. Design critic John Berry called it unusually sinuous, with angles and curves you would not expect and a restrained playfulness, and it holds the distinction of being Terminal Design's first OpenType face to include Cyrillic.

name: Insouciant
classification_notes: Revived and reworked over more than a decade from an earlier custom design, VF Script, for Vanity Fair, itself based on 1920s French automobile poster lettering. Connecting joins were redesigned to solve awkward pairings around r, s, v, w, z and o. Recategorised here as script rather than the original brief's Display label, since this is a connecting cursive design.
summary: A connecting script reworked over more than a decade from 1920s French poster lettering, with alternate b, f and o forms to smooth over its trickiest joins.
description: Insouciant began as VF Script, a custom design for Vanity Fair based on lettering from a 1920s French automobile poster. Montalbano revived and rebuilt it over more than twelve years to solve the connection problems that plagued letters like r, s, v, w, z and o. Ten weights from Extra Thin to Heavy are joined by alternate forms of b, f and o, reached through OpenType stylistic sets.
foundry_blurb: Terminal Design trace Insouciant back to VF Script, a custom design for Vanity Fair based on lettering on a 1920s French automobile poster. The connecting joins caused problems, particularly around r, s, v, w, z and o, and Montalbano spent more than a decade reworking the design, adding alternate b, f and o forms through OpenType stylistic sets.

name: ITC Orbon 2020
classification_notes: Montalbano's first serious typeface design, originally released through ITC in 1995 and reworked in 2020 to fix inconsistencies in the original. A rounded, geometric letterform built for display use.
summary: James Montalbano's first serious typeface design, originally issued through ITC in 1995 and reworked in 2020 to fix the inconsistencies of the original.
description: ITC Orbon 2020 updates Montalbano's earliest professional typeface, accepted by ITC in 1995. The 2020 revision corrects issues he says he has learned to spot since, and expands the character set to cover extended Latin including Vietnamese, Cyrillic and monotonic Greek, across four weights from Light to Black.
foundry_blurb: Terminal Design present ITC Orbon 2020 as an update to Montalbano's first serious typeface, originally accepted by ITC in 1995. He describes the update as correcting some of the inconsistencies of the original design, joking that he has learned a lot since 1995, with the character set expanded considerably while keeping the original's core look.

name: Kaboodle
classification_notes: Drawn from the Clarendon form and 19th and early 20th century wood type. Montalbano dropped an early idea for layered shadow and outline versions in favour of building out a proper weight range instead. Recategorised here as slab rather than the original brief's Script label; Clarendon is a textbook slab-serif model, and nothing in the design is script-like.
summary: A Clarendon-form slab pulled from 19th and early 20th century wood type, built out as a proper four-weight family rather than the layered shadow design Montalbano first sketched.
description: Kaboodle draws on the Clarendon form and historical wood type from the 19th and early 20th centuries. Montalbano first tried it with shadow and outline layers before deciding a real weight range would serve better, drawing the regular first and using it to build the rest. Four weights, Regular to Heavy, each carry an italic, with an unusually wide reach into Cyrillic, Greek and Vietnamese for a slab of this kind.
foundry_blurb: Terminal Design describe Kaboodle as drawing on the Clarendon form and on 19th and early 20th century wood type. Montalbano experimented with layered shadow and outline treatments before deciding it was better to have several weights of the design rather than one weight with fancy layers, drawing the regular first and using it to build the intermediate weights.

name: Kinney
classification_notes: Modelled on C.H. Griffith's Mergenthaler newspaper faces. Built deliberately plain and legible rather than characterful, and originally developed with e-book screens in mind. Recategorised here as serif rather than the original brief's Sans label, since the designer explicitly calls it a serif.
summary: A plain, legible serif modelled on C.H. Griffith's Mergenthaler newspaper faces, built as a serif alternative to the neutral sans serifs that dominate that space.
description: Kinney fills a gap Montalbano saw for a neutral, legible serif in the mould of C.H. Griffith's newspaper designs for Mergenthaler. It was originally developed with e-book screens in mind, and deliberately avoids overt personality in favour of strength and clarity. Six weights from Book to Heavy each include an italic, with small caps, ligatures and a range of figure styles.
foundry_blurb: Terminal Design position Kinney as a serif built to be strong and clear rather than characterful, inspired by C.H. Griffith's newspaper typefaces for Mergenthaler. Montalbano originally developed it for e-book screen display, and offers it as a serif alternative to the popular neutral sans serifs, with small caps, ligatures and a range of figure styles.

name: Latin 512
classification_notes: Montalbano's take on the classical Latin typeface genre, identified by its wedge-shaped serifs. Sold across four widths, standard, compressed, condensed and expanded, and ten weights, an unusually large range for this genre. Recategorised here as serif rather than the original brief's Sans label; the Latin genre is a serif classification defined by its wedge serifs.
summary: An 80-font wedge-serif family across four widths and ten weights, Montalbano's own version of the classical Latin typeface genre.
description: Latin 512 is Montalbano's interpretation of the Latin genre, recognised by its wedge-shaped serifs, and he notes historical accounts disagree on where the name and style even came from. Ten weights from Extra Thin to Black run across four widths, standard, compressed, condensed and expanded, each with italics, for 80 fonts in total, a scale rarely seen in this typeface genre historically.
foundry_blurb: Terminal Design describe Latin 512 as Montalbano's version of the classical Latin typeface genre, marked out by its wedge-shaped serifs. He notes the genre's name has disputed origins, with one account tracing it to Paris's Latin Quarter, though he cannot confirm it. The 80-font family spans four widths and ten weights, a range Montalbano says is historically rare for this genre.

name: Moraine
classification_notes: Originally sketched in a weekend as a teaching tool, then reworked in 2009 to fix excessive contrast and fragility. Wide cupped serifs and tapered stems with no straight lines, in a style the designer calls potentially post-modern rather than tied to one historical model.
summary: A high-contrast serif sketched in a weekend as a teaching exercise, reworked years later to trade its original fragility for a proper weight range.
description: Montalbano first drew Moraine over a weekend, by his own account to embarrass a class of underperforming students into working harder. It sat unused for years until 2009, when he strengthened its excessive contrast and fragile strokes into a proper eight-weight family. Wide cupped serifs and tapered stems avoid straight lines throughout, and the italics were hand-corrected rather than simply slanted, in a style Montalbano calls potentially post-modern.
foundry_blurb: Terminal Design trace Moraine to a design Montalbano sketched over a weekend to embarrass a class of underperforming typeface design students into working harder. He revived and strengthened it in 2009 after years dormant, fixing its original excessive contrast and fragility, and describes the wide cupped serifs, flexed and tapered stems as potentially post-modern, mixing historical details without tying itself to one style.

name: Notary
classification_notes: The designer's own description is the closest thing to a revival I will ever do, based on Ludlow's Record Gothic and the American Gothic trinity of typefaces. Kept close to the original's irregularities rather than corrected, with obliques hand-adjusted rather than mechanically slanted. Recategorised here as sans-serif rather than the original brief's Script label, since this is a gothic sans revival with no script elements.
summary: Montalbano's closest thing to a revival, based on Ludlow's Record Gothic and the American Gothic trinity, kept close to the original's quirks rather than tidied up.
description: Notary is built on Ludlow's Record Gothic and the wider American Gothic family of typefaces. Rather than smoothing out what he saw as irregularities in the source, Montalbano kept them and built a calibrated weight range the original never had. Eight weights from Extra Thin to Heavy include obliques corrected by hand for the optical distortion digital slanting usually causes.
foundry_blurb: Terminal Design call Notary the closest thing to a revival Montalbano will ever do, based on Ludlow's Record Gothic and the American Gothic trinity of typefaces. Rather than correct what he saw as irregularities in the original, he kept to it while adding a carefully calibrated series of weights the source never had, with obliques drawn to fix the optical anomalies caused by digital slanting.

name: Now Playing
classification_notes: A digital revival of naive plastic marquee lettering from Harlem's Apollo Theater, built for the plasma displays installed during its renovation. A single font contains five complete alphabets, caps, lowercase, small caps, superiors and inferiors, and includes logo words that assemble themselves contextually.
summary: A revival of the naive plastic marquee lettering from Harlem's Apollo Theater, drawn for the plasma displays installed in its renovation.
description: Now Playing revives the plastic marquee lettering of the Apollo Theater in Harlem, redrawn for the plasma displays fitted during the venue's renovation. A single font packs in five complete alphabets, caps, lowercase, small caps, superiors and inferiors, along with logo words that assemble themselves automatically depending on context.
foundry_blurb: Terminal Design describe Now Playing as a digital revival of the naive plastic lettering from the Apollo Theater marquee in Harlem, designed for the plasma displays installed during the theater's renovation. It contains five complete alphabets in a single font, uppercase, lowercase, small caps, superior and inferior, plus special logo words that design themselves automatically according to context.

name: Quotient
classification_notes: Uppercase follows Trajan inscriptional proportions, described by the designer as a sort of Trajan Sans, while the lowercase breaks from that tradition. No italic was ever released, as Montalbano was never satisfied with his attempts. Recategorised here as sans-serif rather than the original brief's Serif label, since the design has no serifs.
summary: A ten-weight sans with a Trajan-proportioned uppercase and a lowercase that deliberately breaks from that tradition, released without an italic by design.
description: Montalbano describes Quotient as a bit of a schizophrenic design: the uppercase follows Trajan inscriptional proportions, close to what he calls a Trajan Sans, while the lowercase goes its own way. He tried several italics and stayed unsatisfied with all of them, so the ten-weight family ships roman-only. He suggests all caps for a stately look and lowercase for something more unusual.
foundry_blurb: Terminal Design call Quotient a bit of a schizophrenic design, with an uppercase following Trajan inscriptional proportions, a sort of Trajan Sans, and a lowercase that departs from tradition. Montalbano tried italic versions but stayed unsatisfied with all of them and left them out, suggesting all caps for a stately look and lowercase for something more unusual.

name: Rawlinson 2.0
classification_notes: Grew out of work on the NPS Roadway signage font for the National Park Service, blending elements of Plantin, Sabon and various Garamonds. Unexpectedly produced a usable set of text fonts alongside the signage work. Sold in standard and condensed widths.
summary: An old-style serif that grew out of signage work for the National Park Service, blending Plantin, Sabon and various Garamonds into a large-x-height text face.
description: Rawlinson 2.0 emerged while Montalbano was developing the NPS Roadway font for the National Park Service, gradually mixing in details from Plantin, Sabon and various Garamond designs. What was meant for signage produced, in his words, an unexpectedly useful set of text fonts, with a large x-height for legibility. The National Park Service adopted the design into its identity programme before Montalbano released it commercially, adding small caps and extra figure styles, and it is sold in standard and condensed widths.
foundry_blurb: Terminal Design trace Rawlinson 2.0 to work on the NPS Roadway font for the National Park Service, blending Plantin, Sabon and various Garamond designs. Montalbano notes the signage project unexpectedly produced a set of useful text fonts, adopted by the National Park Service into its identity programme, before he released the design commercially with small caps and several added figure styles.

name: Rawlinson Roadway
classification_notes: An updated, expanded version of Montalbano's original NPS Roadway design, built to replace Clarendon on National Park Service signage. Testing found it 11 percent more legible while taking up 10 to 15 percent less space. Categorised here as sans-serif per house convention, since Roadway is not one of our category options.
summary: An updated version of Montalbano's original NPS Roadway design, built to replace Clarendon on National Park Service signs with better legibility in less space.
description: Rawlinson Roadway updates and expands NPS Roadway, the signage font Montalbano originally developed during a National Park Service identity redesign to replace the Clarendon they had been using. Testing found it out-performed Clarendon by 11 percent in readability while taking up 10 to 15 percent less space. It includes oldstyle figures and small caps, and covers extended Latin for western and central European languages.
foundry_blurb: Terminal Design describe Rawlinson Roadway as Montalbano's updated and expanded version of NPS Roadway, the design he originally developed for the U.S. National Park Service to replace their Clarendon signage font. Testing showed it out-performed the Clarendon by 11 percent in readability while occupying 10 to 15 percent less space, built as a highly readable signage font for wayfinding and park service use.

name: Sensate Delux
classification_notes: Began from a handful of uppercase test characters used to try out new font-making software, later expanded into a full family. The foundry page does not describe its letterform structure in detail; kept as serif per the original brief, with no evidence found to contradict it.
summary: A serif that began as a handful of uppercase test characters for new font-making software, later expanded into a full family with an unusually wide script range.
description: Sensate Delux started, in Montalbano's words, somewhat by accident: a few uppercase characters he kept around to test new font-editing software, expanded into a complete typeface once he had a working beta. Six weights from Light to Black each carry an italic. The Delux tag refers to its extended character set of over 3,000 glyphs, covering Latin, Cyrillic, Greek and the International Phonetic Alphabet.
foundry_blurb: Terminal Design trace Sensate Delux to a few uppercase characters Montalbano kept around to test new font-making software, later expanded while trialling a beta font editor into a complete family. The Delux name marks its extended character set, and reflects Montalbano's interest in the International Phonetic Alphabet, which led him to extend Latin, Cyrillic and Greek support across several of his designs.

name: Shenandoah
classification_notes: Based on wood-routed letters used on signs in Shenandoah National Park, drawn from reference photographs; the uppercase came straight from the reference, with the lowercase drawn separately by Montalbano. The foundry page does not spell out serif or sans terms explicitly; kept as sans per the original brief, consistent with typical routed park-signage lettering.
summary: A rustic signage sans based on wood-routed letters found on signs at Shenandoah National Park, licensed by the National Park Service for use on site.
description: Shenandoah reproduces wood-routed lettering Montalbano found on signs across Shenandoah National Park, sent to him by colleagues at Meeker & Associates. The uppercase came straight from the reference photographs; the lowercase needed extra design work to match. Montalbano finished the project in about a week, and the National Park Service has since licensed it for use in the park.
foundry_blurb: Terminal Design describe Shenandoah as based on wood routed letters used on signs in Shenandoah National Park, drawn from reference photographs supplied by colleagues at Meeker & Associates. Montalbano notes the uppercase was easy since the reference was all there, while the lowercase took extra work; the National Park Service has licensed copies for use at Shenandoah National Park.

name: Slooterdam
classification_notes: Sketched in 2009 and set aside, then finished into a full eight-weight family during the March 2020 pandemic lockdown. Named after the early Dutch settler name for Fair Lawn, New Jersey, Montalbano's hometown, chosen mainly for how it sounds.
summary: A large-x-height contemporary sans first sketched in 2009 and finished into a full eight-weight family during the 2020 lockdown.
description: Montalbano started Slooterdam in 2009 and left it unfinished until the pandemic lockdown of March 2020, when he built out the complete eight-weight family from the original Regular. Its very large x-height led to an unusual approach to small caps, drawn at the same height and weight as the lowercase so they double as alternate lowercase forms. The name comes from the early Dutch settler name for Fair Lawn, New Jersey, Montalbano's hometown.
foundry_blurb: Terminal Design trace Slooterdam to a design Montalbano began in 2009 and set aside until the pandemic lockdown in March 2020, when he developed the complete eight-weight family from an initially drawn Regular. He notes the very large x-height led him to draw small caps at the same height and weight as the lowercase, so they work as both small caps and alternate lowercase forms. The name derives from what early Dutch settlers called Fair Lawn, New Jersey, his hometown, chosen mostly for its sound.

name: Social
classification_notes: Originated as two custom fonts built to harmonise with Living Social's logo, later expanded into a complete retail family once the client's exclusivity period ended. Recategorised here as sans-serif rather than the original brief's Display label, since the designer explicitly calls it the best rounded sans available and it is built to work in text as well as display.
summary: A rounded sans grown from custom logo work for Living Social, with a two-story a as standard and a single-story alternate via stylistic set.
description: Social began as two custom fonts built to sit alongside Living Social's logo, and was expanded into a full retail family once the client's one-year exclusive period ended. Montalbano built the roman on upright italic forms, which made drawing the italic straightforward. Eight weights from Thin to Heavy include a two-story a with a single-story alternate, small caps and multiple figure styles, and it marked his first retail release with Vietnamese support.

name: Tangent
classification_notes: Developed through Montalbano's teaching, built specifically to avoid the perfect circles and squares that he argues make for poor-looking geometric sans letterforms.
summary: A geometric sans deliberately drawn to avoid the perfect circles and squares that make most geometric sans letterforms look mechanical.
description: Tangent came out of Montalbano's work teaching type design, built around the idea that perfect circles and squares make terrible-looking letters. Eight weights from Thin to Black, each with a matching oblique, minimise the pure geometric forms typical of the genre in favour of something friendlier and more legible.
foundry_blurb: Terminal Design present Tangent as friendly and legible in both text and display, carefully drawn to minimise the pure geometric forms typical of geometric sans serifs, since Montalbano holds that perfect circles and squares make terrible looking letters. He offers it as a lively alternate to the overused designs that dominate the geometric sans category.

name: Trilon
classification_notes: Designed at a friend's request for something without the droopy shoulders of American Gothics or the fatigue of European Gothics. Carries a subtle squareness without tipping into full geometric severity. Sold across four widths, regular, compressed, condensed and expanded, with four OpenType stylistic sets altering the g, a and y.
summary: An 80-font grotesque sans across four widths and ten weights, drawn to avoid both the droopy shoulders of American Gothics and the fatigue of European ones.
description: Trilon was built at the request of a friend tired of the droopy shoulders in American Gothic sans faces and equally tired of the European Gothics. The result carries a subtle squareness without becoming a full geometric design, across ten weights and four widths, regular, compressed, condensed and expanded, all with obliques. Four OpenType stylistic sets shift the g, a and y between different personalities.

The result carries a subtle squareness without excessive geometric severity, and the complete 80-font family spans weights and widths with obliques, plus four OpenType stylistic sets that modify the lowercase g, a and y.

name: VF Sans
classification_notes: Designed for Vanity Fair magazine in the late 1990s, drawing on 1930s sans-serif models and compared by others to Intertype's Vogue, though that was not the intent. Kept proprietary for twelve years before release to retail, with a condensed width and Ultra Thin weights added at that point.
summary: A 1930s-inspired sans built for Vanity Fair in the late 1990s, kept proprietary for over a decade before its retail release.
description: Montalbano designed VF Sans for Vanity Fair in the late 1990s, drawing on 1930s sans-serif models; it has been compared to Intertype's Vogue, though that was not a deliberate reference. The magazine kept it exclusive for twelve years before losing interest as it appeared less often in the pages, at which point Montalbano released it commercially with permission, adding Ultra Thin weights, a condensed width and a full set of obliques.
foundry_blurb: Terminal Design describe VF Sans as created for Vanity Fair magazine in the late 1990s, drawing on 1930s sans-serif designs; Montalbano notes it has been compared to Intertype's Vogue, though unintentionally. After twelve years of proprietary use, Vanity Fair's interest faded, and with permission he released the family commercially, adding Ultra Thin weights and a complete oblique set.

name: Yo
classification_notes: A Didone family in the Didot/Bodoni tradition, built as a width system rather than a conventional weight family: each of twenty numbered cuts, One to Twenty, is available with italics, and five of those width points are sold as named, independent complete families, Yo Andy (narrowest), Yo Frankie, Yo Lucy, Yo Sophie and Yo Zelda (widest), with Andy naming the letter closest to the front of the alphabet for the narrowest width and Zelda the widest. The original brief listed only Yo Andy as a Sans family; this corrects both the category, which is serif, and the scope, since Frankie, Lucy, Sophie and Zelda are separate named products within the same system not mentioned in the original list.
summary: A Didone super-family built as a width system rather than a weight system, sold as five named cuts running from the narrow Yo Andy to the wide Yo Zelda.
description: Yo is Montalbano's Didone design, in the Didot and Bodoni tradition, taken apart along a width axis instead of the usual weight axis. Twenty numbered cuts, One to Twenty, each with an italic, run from narrow to wide, and five points along that range are sold as their own named complete families: Yo Andy at the narrowest end, Yo Zelda at the widest, with Yo Lucy in the middle and Yo Frankie and Yo Sophie between them. Montalbano has said a name starting with A sits at the narrow end and one starting with Z at the wide end, by design.
foundry_blurb: Terminal Design frame the Yo family around a simple naming logic: a name beginning with the letter A is the narrowest cut and one beginning with Z the widest, so Yo Andy and Yo Zelda sit at the extremes, Yo Lucy in the middle, and Yo Frankie and Yo Sophie in between. What began as a 100-font super-family grew to 200 fonts once italics were added across all twenty numbered widths.
